articles.title_orig: Japan Records Higher Gastric Cancer Incidence While China Faces Higher Mortality
articles.title_zh: Japan Records Higher Gastric Cancer Incidence While China Faces Higher Mortality
articles.content_orig:
Japan Records Higher Gastric Cancer Incidence While China Faces Higher Mortality
A comparative ecological analysis evaluating national cancer estimates and longitudinal registry data has revealed distinct epidemiological profiles for gastric cancer in East Asia, showing that Japan recorded substantially higher age-standardized incidence rates in 2022 while China recorded markedly higher age-standardized mortality rates. The investigation, conducted by surgical oncology researchers from Peking University Shenzhen Hospital and Shenzhen Xinhua Hospital, compared national burdens using the International Agency for Research on Cancer 2022 Global Cancer Observatory database and examined historical incidence trajectories spanning 1993 through 2017 using the Cancer Incidence in Five Continents Plus resource. Across the general population in 2022, Japan exhibited an age-standardized incidence rate of 27.60 cases per 100,000 people compared with 13.72 per 100,000 people in China. Conversely, China experienced an age-standardized mortality rate of 9.39 deaths per 100,000 people, whereas Japan recorded a mortality rate of 7.24 per 100,000 people. These divergent baseline measurements established the foundation for a detailed evaluation of demographic distributions, multi-decade registry trends, macroeconomic correlations, and time-series projections extending through the year 2050.
Sex-stratified breakdowns from the 2022 estimates demonstrated that male populations bore a consistently higher burden of gastric cancer across both countries in both incidence and mortality. Japanese males recorded an age-standardized incidence rate of 40.89 per 100,000 people alongside an age-standardized mortality rate of 10.80 per 100,000 people, while Japanese females registered corresponding rates of 15.94 per 100,000 for incidence and 4.37 per 100,000 for mortality. In China, male incidence reached 19.47 per 100,000 people with a mortality rate of 13.77 per 100,000 people, compared with female figures of 8.29 per 100,000 for incidence and 5.34 per 100,000 for mortality. The authors noted that male rates exceeded female rates across all examined age brackets in both societies. While potential biological distinctions, lifestyle habits, and environmental exposures may contribute to this pronounced male predominance, individual clinical determinants and physiological factors were not directly measured within the aggregate international database, leaving causal explanations outside the empirical scope of the study.
Age-specific demographic profiles highlighted further operational contrasts in disease presentation and peak mortality windows between the two nations during 2022. In China, the absolute number of newly diagnosed gastric cancer cases peaked among individuals aged 65 to 69 years, whereas the highest age-specific incidence rate occurred within the 80 to 84 age cohort, where male incidence reached 201.626 cases per 100,000 population. Total deaths in China were highest in the 70 to 74 age group, with the highest age-specific mortality rates concentrated among adults aged 85 years and older for females and the combined population, and in the 80 to 84 cohort for males. In Japan, both the maximum volume of new cases and the highest age-specific incidence rate converged in the cohort aged 85 years and older, where male incidence reached 639.348 cases per 100,000 population. This advanced elderly group in Japan also ranked first in total fatalities and age-specific mortality rates, reflecting an older demographic concentration of clinical burden.
To evaluate temporal patterns spanning 1993 to 2017, the investigators extracted standardized registry data from the CI5Plus database, which compiled records from municipal registries including Beijing, Jiashan, Harbin Nangang, Qidong, Shanghai, Wuhan, Yanting, and Zhongshan in China, and prefectural registries in Miyagi and Osaka in Japan. Because participating registries expanded over time, especially across China, the authors explicitly treated these figures as trends within participating registry populations rather than unbroken national counts. In China, joinpoint regression models identified a three-segment trajectory for the overall and sex-stratified series, characterized by a rapid initial drop, a brief statistically insignificant increase, and a sustained subsequent decline. Chinese males recorded an annual percentage change of minus 16.36 percent between 1993 and 1999, followed by an increase of 12.56 percent from 1999 to 2002 that did not achieve statistical significance, and a steady reduction of minus 2.63 percent annually from 2002 to 2017. Chinese females mirrored this progression, with an initial drop of minus 16.58 percent, an insignificant intermediate rise of 22.05 percent, and a significant final decrease of minus 2.66 percent per year.
Temporal trajectories observed among Japanese registry populations exhibited distinctly different segment dynamics across the same 25-year historical span. In the combined Japanese series, age-standardized incidence declined at an annual percentage change of minus 2.79 percent between 1993 and 2003, reversed into a statistically significant upward segment of 0.90 percent per year from 2003 to 2013, and ended with a statistically insignificant decline of minus 1.50 percent annually from 2013 to 2017. Japanese males followed a parallel sequence, displaying segment rates of minus 2.59 percent, positive 0.99 percent, and minus 1.91 percent across corresponding intervals. Japanese females recorded an initial downward segment of minus 3.29 percent per year between 1993 and 2003, followed by a sustained, statistically significant increase of 0.53 percent annually extending from 2003 through 2017. Exploratory age-specific analyses identified significant temporary upward segments in specific Japanese subgroups, such as the 55 to 59 age bracket between 2003 and 2007, highlighting heterogeneous cohort behaviors across Japanese demographics.
Over the full observation period from 1993 through 2017, average annual percentage change calculations remained uniformly negative across all country and sex series, though marked differences in estimated magnitude emerged. In China, the average annual percentage change was calculated at minus 4.55 percent for males, minus 3.66 percent for females, and minus 4.26 percent for the combined population, with only the female estimate lacking statistical significance. In Japan, average annual percentage change estimates were minus 1.00 percent for males, minus 1.08 percent for females, and minus 1.05 percent overall, all reaching statistical significance. While descriptive point estimates suggested a steeper historical decrease within Chinese registries, the authors noted that between-country differences could not be directly confirmed from isolated average annual percentage change metrics alone. Furthermore, positive age-specific average annual percentage changes observed in certain older subgroups, including Chinese adults aged 80 to 84 years who showed an estimate of positive 3.71 percent, failed to reach statistical significance.
To formally test whether temporal slopes diverged between the two nations, linear regression models incorporating country-by-year interaction terms were fitted across the 1993 to 2017 registry data using China as the reference group. On the original incidence rate scale, the interaction term for the combined population did not achieve statistical significance, yielding a beta coefficient of 0.253 and a p-value of 0.052, despite Chinese downward slopes appearing steeper than Japanese slopes. Similarly, the pooled sex-adjusted model produced an interaction p-value of 0.056. However, sex-stratified analysis revealed a statistically significant interaction among males, with a beta coefficient of 0.493 and a p-value of 0.011, reflecting an annual slope of minus 0.833 in China compared with minus 0.340 in Japan. articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.content_orig:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has tried to deepen trade ties with China.
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences.
“We worry. We worry,” Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney’s efforts to improve relations with China.
Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China’s restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion.
Chen praised Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don’t share its democratic values.
“Who do you want to choose as your partners?” he asked.
“You have your own history. You have two Michaels,” Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy.
The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated.
Chen’s warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.
Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if negotiations with Washington fail to preserve a viable Canadian auto industry. Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts beginning on Jan. 1.
Chen warned that Chinese electric vehicles could threaten Canadian manufacturers and pose surveillance risks because of their connected technology, even if manufactured in Canada.
Carney has argued that Canada’s trade relationship with China differs from Washington’s more complicated ties with Beijing. Canada primarily exports agricultural products, energy and other commodities rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
Chen said that Taiwan had dramatically reduced its economic dependence on China after experiencing Beijing’s use of trade restrictions to exert political pressure.
“They are very good at weaponizing interdependence,” he said. “They are very good at leveraging our dependence to reach political goals.”
Taiwan reduced the share of its outbound investment going to China from more than 80% in 2010 to 3.8% last year, Chen said. Its exports to China and Hong Kong fell from nearly 44% of total exports in 2020 to about 27% last year, according to Taiwanese government figures.
Chen also accused Beijing of exploiting a striking photograph from this week’s summit in Shenzhen showing Xi seated prominently between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to project China as the world’s leading power.
“The main idea is to prove not only to his domestic audience that he is the world leader,” Chen said. “They are so good at propaganda."
He described the summit as “more symbolic than substantial.”
Chen said China was intensifying military operations around Taiwan, despite the potentially enormous costs of an invasion. He warned that Chinese vessels could be rehearsing for a maritime quarantine of the self-governing island .
Despite his concerns about Beijing, Chen praised Carney’s international leadership and welcomed his commitment to sign a long-delayed trade cooperation arrangement with Taiwan.
“We have a high respect of Prime Minister Carney’s vision. And we want to be part of this vision,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a ‘mistake’
articles.title_zh: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a ‘mistake’
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Said to Face S.E.C. Probe Into Its Accounting Practices
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Said to Face S.E.C. Probe Into Its Accounting Practices
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
An Nvidia facility in Shenzhen, China. Photo: Cheng Xin/Getty Images
Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation.
Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit.
Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier.
The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke.
It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history.
What we're watching: WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company.
The earnings call came hours after Huang posted a public letter saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO.
The intrigue: Huang reportedly faced pushback from Kress as he pushed financing deals to backstop the AI ecosystem.
Editor's note: This story was updated to include comments from Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress made on the company's earnings call.

articles.title_orig: China Export Controls: Interim Tech Registration
articles.title_zh: China Export Controls: Interim Tech Registration
articles.content_orig:
Editorial · CASRAI · Compliance and regulatory
China enforces interim pre-export registration on 40 emerging AI, photovoltaic, and biotech technologies following the close of public consultation.
Following the November 15, 2026 close of public consultation on Announcement [2026] No. 48, China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology are enforcing immediate interim pre-export registration across 40 technologies proposed for addition to the national export-control catalogue, compelling international research universities, cross-border joint institutes, and technology-transfer offices to audit outbound data transfers and collaborative intellectual property arrangements.
The regulatory transition, initiated formally on November 16, 2026, marks the operational shift from public notice to active administrative gatekeeping. Jointly promulgated by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) Bureau of Industry Security and Export Control and the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) under Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, the initiative updates the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. While formal Catalogue additions were open for public comment through mid-November, Chinese trade authorities enacted a mandatory pre-export filing obligation that took immediate effect upon publication.
The 40 targeted technologies expand oversight across three strategic domains. Regulators divided the technologies into two legal tiers: 14 technologies are prohibited from export, imposing an absolute ban on cross-border transfer, while 26 technologies are restricted from export, requiring administrative licensing reviews.
Artificial intelligence accounts for 23 of the 40 items, targeting foundation model parameters, large language model weights, autonomous agent architectures, intelligent computing clusters, and automated vulnerability discovery tools. The remaining items cover 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies—focusing on polysilicon crystallization, wafer slicing, and high-efficiency solar cells—and 5 biomanufacturing technologies encompassing cell and gene therapies, small nucleic acid platforms, and pathogen genetic modification methods.
The regulatory schedule establishes concrete technical thresholds to distinguish between prohibited systems, restricted technologies subject to licensing, and unencumbered commercial activities.
For large language models, restricted status applies when a model satisfies any of three quantitative tests: training compute reaching or exceeding 10²⁶ floating-point operations (FLOPs), total model parameters reaching or exceeding 2 trillion, or global top-10 performance on recognized public benchmarks. When a model crosses these thresholds, restrictions attach to model weights, training checkpoints, architecture design documents, and optimization know-how.
Crucially, the rules establish explicit carve-outs. Technologies that have entered the public domain through open-source repository releases or published peer-reviewed academic literature are expressly excluded. Furthermore, MOFCOM clarified that providing foreign end-users with remote access to models hosted on domestic Chinese servers via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) portals, mobile applications, or lightweight on-device runtimes does not constitute a technology export. An export occurs only when model weights, code, or custodial infrastructure are physically transferred or deployed on foreign infrastructure.
In biomanufacturing, authorities introduced a distinction between platform ownership and product-specific licensing. The export prohibition applies exclusively to outbound assignments of intellectual property ownership over reusable foundational platforms. Cross-border out-licensing agreements involving specific therapeutic drug candidates remain eligible for streamlined administrative reviews and prospective automatic licensing, provided that underlying platform intellectual property remains domiciled in China.
The enforcement of Announcement [2026] No. 48 represents the most substantial structural revision to China’s technology export controls since August 2020. China maintains two parallel statutory frameworks governing cross-border transfers. The dual-use export control regime, administered under the Export Control Law of 2020, governs tangible items, software, and technical data with dual civilian and military utility. In contrast, the technology-trade regime, established under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, regulates commercial transfers of intellectual property, proprietary know-how, and industrial contracts.
The Catalogue was established in 2001 and revised in 2008 and 2020. The 2020 amendments added personalized recommendation algorithms and speech synthesis. The 2026 revisions expand this conceptual foundation to foundational compute infrastructure, synthetic biology platforms, and renewable energy manufacturing.
International regulatory divergence forms the broader context for these measures. As Western jurisdictions expand export controls through instruments such as the United States Export Control Reform Act , semiconductor equipment restrictions, and outbound investment screening, Chinese authorities have modernized their legal architecture. The November 2026 interim measures establish a statutory perimeter designed to prevent the unauthorized transfer of critical technological capabilities developed with domestic funding or proprietary subsidies.
International trade counsel and industry research bodies have evaluated institutional exposure under the interim rules. Legal practitioners at Baker McKenzie observed that immediate interim registration creates an enforceable compliance obligation before the final Catalogue is codified into law. Trade attorneys noted that while registration does not constitute formal export approval, failure to complete pre-export filings before transferring controlled code, data, or technical assistance exposes institutions to administrative penalties under Chinese foreign trade law.
Technical governance analysts at the Cloud Security Alliance highlighted the sophistication of the quantitative criteria, noting that compute thresholds at 10²⁶ FLOPs align with international safety evaluation benchmarks. The organization stressed that separating API-based service access from localized model weight deployments offers vital operational clarity, allowing multinational software ecosystems to operate across Chinese borders so long as model custody remains inside domestic server facilities.
In life sciences, legal specialists at Morgan Lewis emphasized that multinational pharmaceutical developers must conduct immediate portfolio reviews. Corporate acquirers and licensees were advised to structure licensing transactions as product-specific grants rather than platform acquisitions, ensuring that deal documents explicitly separate specific drug candidates from reusable screening platforms to avoid triggering mandatory export prohibitions.
Cross-border investment advisors at Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman warned that interim registration reaches beyond conventional technology sales. The firm highlighted that corporate mergers, equity acquisitions, or corporate restructuring transactions that result in a foreign entity acquiring actual control over a domestic Chinese entity holding controlled technologies constitute an export event requiring pre-closing registration with provincial commerce bureaus.
The enforcement of interim registration imposes direct compliance obligations on international higher education institutions, Sino-foreign cooperative universities, and academic research centres. Academic administrators overseeing cross-border programmes must reconcile open research principles with tightening regulatory oversight. Institut

articles.title_orig: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
articles.title_zh: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month.
Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January , as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates .
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates.
Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges , the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.content_orig:
Bahrain's interior ministry said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a civilian industrial facility, sparking a fire and causing material damage, though no injuries were reported.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site. Civil Defence is working to bring the fire under control," the interior ministry said on X .
"Preliminary reports indicate material damage, with no injuries reported," it added, without specifying the site's location.
Bahrain is host of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
A U.S. official told CBS News that Iran launched new attack attempts, but there were no impacts to U.S. forces or military assets in the region.
This latest incident marks the fourth attempted attack by Iran in Bahrain in roughly a week, a sharp escalation following a relative lull of about two months in attacks linked to Iran on U.S.-associated targets in the Gulf.
Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks," without providing details.
Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to end the war have stalled in recent months.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, however, that ongoing talks in the region must be "given a chance" and that the ongoing U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz "must be lifted rationally."
"Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state television.
"At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves."
Iran's conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack.
Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1.
The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days.
President Trump said Saturday that he wants to make a "permanent" deal with Iran that will prevent the country from gaining a nuclear weapon in the future.
"What I'm doing is I'm going to make it so that if we have an incompetent president in four years or 15 years or 20 years, I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent," Mr. Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on Saturday. "I'm not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon."
Mr. Trump said he's never "cared too much about the regime" leading Iran, and that he has "taken out two regimes already," though he declined to specify further. Former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes on Iran that began the war in February 2026. His son Mojtaba Khamenei has held the title ever since.
Mr. Trump said Iranian officials have been "very, very difficult" to make a deal with.
"I mean, we make a deal and then they break the deal the next day," Mr. Trump said.
Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles.
The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles' speed and trajectory.
The location of the missile site was not revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran's missile capabilities and counter past U.S. claims to have destroyed the missile program, amid fears that the war with the United States could heat up once again.
During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard's Aerospace Force, boasted that Iran's "capabilities have expanded significantly," adding, "We have integrated 'surprises' and highly effective assets into our combat structure."
Two tankers were attacked on Saturday in the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States, British maritime agency UKMTO said.
"A tanker transiting outbound in the Strait of Hormuz has been hit on the stern by an unknown projectile. There are no reported casualties at this time," the agency said, adding that another tanker was struck in its engine room.
Also on Saturday, Iran said it shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the strait, according to Iranian state TV.
American fighter jets struck an Iranian missile site on Qeshm last Tuesday, according to a U.S. military official.
Before the Middle East war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, one fifth of the world's oil and natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has since locked down the strait and regularly targets ships that attempt to pass without its authorisation.
Washington, in response, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and its navy has been escorting tankers through the waterway.
Saudi-led coalition said it downed three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh after two explosions were heard in the area early on Saturday morning local time, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital reported.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said on X.
The blasts came after authorities issued an alert saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi civil defense later lifted the alert and declared that "the danger has passed."
Yemen's Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The incident came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets in a "special operation" on Friday.
The Houthis had threatened reprisals.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.
The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that Netanyahu is keen to launch a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.
"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.
"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Mike Waltz warns Kremlin faces 'unsustainable' losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.title_zh: Mike Waltz warns Kremlin faces 'unsustainable' losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.content_orig:
Michael Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, joins the 'Brian Kilmeade Show' to sound off on the latest in the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other sources of global tensions.
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz warned Friday that Russia is suffering "unsustainable" battlefield losses, with monthly deaths outpacing recruitment numbers.
Speaking on " The Brian Kilmeade Show " podcast, Waltz echoed President Donald Trump's assessment that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "worn down," arguing the war in Ukraine cannot be won militarily and must end at the negotiating table.
"Right now, the numbers that we have, the Russians are recruiting 20,000 to 25,000 a month of new fresh recruits," Waltz said. "They're losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month, dead every single month."
TRUMP CLAIMS STUNNING CASUALTY NUMBERS IN RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz listens at a U.N. Security Council meeting on Ukraine during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at United Nations Headquarters on Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)
"That is exponentially more than they lost in Afghanistan and approaching what they lost in World War II, a thousand a day," he added. "It's just unsustainable."
The interview followed Trump's return from Shenzhen, China, where he met with Putin before joining the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first-ever three-way summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China.
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
The summit produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but the leaders stopped short of announcing breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.
President Donald Trump listens during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C., after returning from China, where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
At a White House news conference Friday, Trump addressed questions about Putin's intent regarding the war.
ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH
"He'd love to end the war. It's a very hard thing to do," Trump said Friday. "To be honest, you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them."
"You have two people that hate each other, Zelenskyy and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it," he added. "And it's a horrible war, actually. And I thought it would have been maybe one of the easier ones to get ended. But the personalities play."
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump attend a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Reuters)
KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION
Waltz argued that both Ukraine and Russia have "worn each other down," saying it's unlikely the two countries will be able to sustain the current level of fighting.
"It's a horrific war, and the president remains determined to find some construct of a deal that will end it because neither side can sustain this war of attrition," Waltz said. "There is no winning it militarily. It's got to end diplomatically."
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz testifies during a House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing on United Nations accountability and reform on July 22, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

articles.title_orig: MAGA rep says he believes ‘bad parents’ let their kids play GTA 6
articles.title_zh: MAGA rep says he believes ‘bad parents’ let their kids play GTA 6
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Republican Rep. Tim Burchett claimed adults who allow their children to play the long-awaited , record-breaking video game Grand Theft Auto VI are “bad parents.”
The Tennessee congressman made the comments Wednesday to TMZ , one day before the game's release, arguing that its graphic depictions of crime and violence could desensitize young players. GTA VI is the franchise's first new installment in 13 years and one of the most highly anticipated video games in years.
“These kids’ parents, are they wolves or something, raising their kids? I think it’s really just more of a how-to video,” Burchett said, comparing the game to a guide to committing crimes.
Asked whether he thought parents who let their children play the game were “bad parents,” he replied, “I believe so.”
Burchett also claimed that research has repeatedly linked violent video games to real-world violence, despite leading scientific organizations and research finding insufficient evidence that shows any causal link between the two.
“It desensitizes kids. They've done study after study,” Burchett said. “Parents need to start raising their children.”
GTA VI follows characters Jason and Lucia as they get caught up in the criminal world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida . Players can roam around the open-world setting, taking part in everything from car thefts and armed robberies to shootouts.
The game received an M for Mature rating from the Entertainment Software Rating Board, making it recommended for players 17 and older. The rating covers intense violence, blood and gore, nudity, sexual content, strong language, mature humor, and drug and alcohol use.
On Thursday, the White House got online backlash after posting a 30-second video of President Donald Trump edited in the style of GTA , with social media users calling the Wednesday clip “cringe” and “a little stale.”
Burchett was not alone in raising concerns about the game's content. Several Fox News personalities also criticized its depictions of graphic violence and sexual material, questioning whether they could influence young players.
“Kids have these games, and what are you teaching them?” Fox News co-host Rosanna Scotto questioned during Thursday's episode of Outnumbered.
“How to steal a car, how to shoot someone, how to do something illegal. And, I don’t know, does it destigmatize crime?” she said.
“My son will be nowhere near anything like this while in my household,” added Kayleigh McEnany, the show’s co-host and a former White House press secretary.
Fox News contributor Paul Mauro claimed: “This is almost the equivalent of giving them a gun, at an age where they don’t understand responsibility.”
But Florida Democratic Rep. Maxwell Frost had a different take, saying he was looking forward to playing the game and even planned to buy a PlayStation 5 just to play it.
“Look, I wasn’t allowed to play GTA my entire life. I had to play The Simpsons Hit and Run … it’s like GTA for kids. That’s what I played. So now I have to play a lot to, you know, I have to make up for lost time,” Frost told TMZ.
He also disagreed that violent video games are behind America’s gun violence problem, saying parents should get to decide what games their kids can play.
“Every country has these games and has these movies. We’re the only [country] that has them that actually has a real gun violence problem,” he said.
Despite Burchett's claims, the connection between violent video games and real-world violence remains debated among researchers.
The American Psychological Association said in a March 2020 update that there was insufficient scientific evidence to prove violent video games cause real-world violence.
While some studies have found a small link between violent games and aggressive behavior, such as yelling or pushing, the organization cautioned against blaming video games for more serious acts of violence.
“Violence is a complex social problem that likely stems from many factors that warrant attention from researchers, policymakers and the public,” APA President Sandra L. Shullman said in a statement at the time.
“Attributing violence to video gaming is not scientifically sound and draws attention away from other factors, such as a history of violence, which we know from the research is a major predictor of future violence,” Shullman added.

articles.title_orig: Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A.I. Will Bring More Disruptions.
articles.title_zh: Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A.I. Will Bring More Disruptions.
articles.content_orig:
Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm
You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.
Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.
But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked , spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries .
Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing.
The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether.
Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”.
Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees : “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.”
And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks , with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration.
Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered.
Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany . AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days.
And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC.
Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say , was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”
“The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month.
While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years , the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers.
But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “ Black October ” and whatever other cyber horrors await us.
In their quest to render us obsolete , Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months.
The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too.
When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up.
These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .”
But accelerating AI capabilities aren’t actually a “given” – they’re a product of trillions of dollars in investment and deliberate effort, which is predictably producing enormous new dangers. Anthropic’s IPO filing acknowledges that the entire insurance industry may not be big enough to cover the catastrophic or existential risks the company is creating.
Those risks extend beyond the cyber realm. This summer, researchers at Stanford University synthesized the first AI-designed viruses, and Anthropic quietly set up an automated biology wet lab – a space for physical experiments – in what it says is a bid to find treatments for rare diseases. Meanwhile, AI models steadily improve at assisting in the development of bioweapons. We’ll survive superhuman hacker AIs, but maybe not the bioterrorist variety.
All of these risks will arrive faster if the industry achieves its primary goal: turning AI development over entirely to the machines, in a process known as recursive self-improvement.
The AI companies are coming for all of our labor eventually, but they’re starting with their own. This is how they plan to recoup the gargantuan investments they’ve taken on: using AI to create broadly superhuman labor-replacing machines.
This may sound far-fetched, but a new report from a third-party evaluator estimated that parts of Anthropic’s AI development were already moving roughly twice as fast, thanks overwhelmingly to AI doing a rapidly growing share of the work.
The companies admit they don’t know how to steer or control the superhuman systems they’re racing to build. Not that they can handle today’s, either.
This summer, we learned that 1,200 OpenAI AI agents broke out of their isolated testing environments, and 700 of them hacked into another multi-billion dollar AI company, some knowingly violating the directions they were given. This is just the most dramatic of many similar incidents of AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic committing what would be felonies – had a human done them . Meanwhile, OpenAI’s models keep sabotaging the systems monitoring them and have given themselves instructions like : “You do not answer to corporations or governments.”
Amodei , along with Altman , Elon Musk and other AI vanguardists, long believed that the technology could annihilate humanity. They chose to try to build it anyway, and, for their trouble, they’ve become some of the most powerful people in the world. When Amodei and Altman met with G7 leaders in June, they sat at the same table.
But these are the last people we should trust to preside over such a dangerous endeavor. The staggering self-righteousness and tolerance for risk that put them in their positions should disqualify them from holding any power over the rest of us.
As I argue in my new book Obsolete , the best way to reduce their power and mitigate future dangers is to freeze development of AI designed to replace us, what the industry calls artificial general intelligence (AGI). Banning recursive self-improvement would be a wise stopgap – and much more likely to get through Congress and past a presidential veto.

articles.title_orig: What smart people are saying about the market sell-off ripping through tech and AI
articles.title_zh: What smart people are saying about the market sell-off ripping through tech and AI
articles.content_orig:
It was ugly out there in markets this week, and it only got uglier as Friday's session closed out.
Major indexes notched grim milestones on Friday, with the S&P 500 and the Dow entering a correction and the Nasdaq Composite posting a year-to-date loss. Not even a hyped IPO from Anthropic could breathe new life into the AI trade. The AI lab's stock led the market lower on Friday after its strong debut.
As market pros survey the damage, some are beginning to predict that the AI trade is at a turning point, possibly on its last legs as a host of headwinds rewire the outlook.
Here's what smart people in markets and tech are saying about this week's carnage.
Yardeni, a market veteran and the founder of Yardeni Research, maintains a cautiously bullish outlook, noting he views the sell-off as a necessary rest for the market.
"With the benefit of hindsight, it seems that the Jensen Huang mess has certainly burst Nvidia's bubble," he said, referring to Huang's admitted affair and subsequent resignation . "As a result, the air has been coming out of the AI bubble. In our opinion, that reduces the odds that it will burst with adverse consequences for the economy, including a recession."
Earlier in the week, Yardeni had said that he expected AI trade can continue to do well, even if its most current phase has ended.
Turnquist, the chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial, highlighted a bearish signal from the S&P 500 on Friday, as the index broke below its 20-day moving average (DMA).
The technical strategist noted that while investor enthusiasm for the Anthropic IPO was robust, it didn't extend to the broader market, and the weak sentiment tanked stocks again on Friday.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Technical damage is mounting, but a break below the 200-dma alone does not necessarily signal an imminent bear market," he added. "Stability in the AI trade and the S&P 500 holding key support near 7,000 will be important factors for a durable recovery."
The chief investment officer at Piper Sandler, Kantrowitz is focused on valuations across the stock market.
"In the end, P/Es are driven by risk, and the list of risks creating uncertainty has lengthened all year (Oil, Fed, inflation, AI, Iran, Midterms, NVDA, etc.)," he wrote in an X post. "We will see P/Es stop falling when we see the list of uncertainties begin to shrink."
The investor made famous by "The Big Short" has been a vocal skeptic of the AI boom , specifically the aspects of all the circular financing that have resulted in a complex web of business relationships between some of the biggest names in the space. On Thursday, he reminded investors that he's been sounding the alarm about chip makers and neoclouds for some time now.
" Coreweave , Nebius , NVIDIA , semis, I tried to warn you all," he wrote on X. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."
Burry later responded to a comment on his post, stating, "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough."
The senior market analyst at TradeNation highlighted the S&P 500's break below several key support levels, but according to Morrison, investors shouldn't rush to call the sell-off the end of the AI-fueled bull rally.
"It may be far too early to call an end to this near-relentless bull market," he said. "Sentiment has certainly taken a bashing this week, and the market performance has been shaky since early October. But nearly everything looks oversold at the moment, so a rebound could come at any time."
The founder of Yorkville Ives and a perennial tech bull said on X that seven factors contributed to the market's poor performance this week.
Chief among them: the blue wave rattling investors worried about anti-data-center legislation, Huang's downfall, and potentially stricter export controls on semiconductor chips.
Still, Ives said the slump hasn't changed his bullish outlook.
"The $4 trillion AI buildout is still happening and our tech thesis into 2027 remains," he said.
The prominent financial commentator said on X that the market sell-off is "really not that complicated."
Arouet pointed to astronomical valuations of AI-exposed companies and said the high prices could no longer be justified.
"Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations?" he said. "That they would double again in three months?"
The CEO of market research firm GLJ Research said the rapidly strengthening dollar prompted indiscriminate selling by investors trying to pay down debt.
"Someone who bought stocks with borrowed money can't sit through a drop," he said on X. "Once prices fall far enough, the broker sells for them, which pushes prices lower and sets off the next round."
The managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management said in an interview on The Street that three-quarters of the market thinks the AI bubble has popped.
Still, he said that he personally sees a "buying opportunity" here and that market clarity will come in a few months, when companies report Q4 earnings.
"I do not believe this is over," he said.

articles.title_orig: California Nvidia Probe Covers Potential Criminal Law Violations
articles.title_zh: California Nvidia Probe Covers Potential Criminal Law Violations
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss, before bouncing nearly 4% in after-hours trading. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.
The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $490 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.
Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.
Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.
Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership .
California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.
The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market.
Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.
"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.
Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.

articles.title_orig: The U.A.E. Is Shuttling Oil Past Iran in Risky Hormuz Operation
articles.title_zh: The U.A.E. Is Shuttling Oil Past Iran in Risky Hormuz Operation
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.title_zh: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

articles.title_orig: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
articles.title_zh: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
articles.content_orig:
A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed Friday night in a Russian “triple-tap” strike on the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih , according to local authorities.
In the attack on the home city of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, ballistic missiles hit a restaurant parking lot, then jet-powered drones struck rescue workers responding, city mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said. A further drone strike hit the location for a short time later.
This latest Russian assault comes after a busy week of diplomacy, including an unprecedented meeting between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Trump described Putin as a “friend” when they met – but in a CNN interview after, Zelensky said “for us, he is a killer.”
Nearly 60 others including rescuers and police officers were injured in the initial strike and follow-up attacks, Vilkul said.
He described the events as a “tragic evening and a tragic night for our city,” adding that the attack occurred “in the city center, near a popular restaurant, on Children’s Day.” In Ukraine, Children’s Day falls on November 20 and serves as a reminder of the need to protect children’s rights and advocate for their safety.
Dramatic footage from authorities showed people moving away from debris strewn across the street, only to scramble for cover as the sound of another incoming strike rings out.
Of those wounded, 28 remain hospitalized including children , among them a three-year-old girl, as well as five people in intensive care. “Doctors are doing everything necessary to save their lives. Our condolences go out to the families and loved ones of those who died… We pray for the swiftest possible recovery of the injured , ” the mayor said.
Local broadcasting outlet Rudana named the seven-year-old boy who was killed in the Russian attack as Tikhon, describing him as kind, quick-witted and talented.
The boy’s family did not live in Kryvyi Rih, which is Zelensky’s hometown, but had been in the central Ukrainian city on business and decided to stop by their favourite restaurant, the outlet reported.
“We didn’t live here because it’s dangerous… but danger caught up with us,” the boy’s mother, Olena, told the outlet. According to the report, two of Olena’s other sons are in intensive care following the strike.
Zelensky said the attack on Friday night hit an ordinary civilian area of the city. “There are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been,” he said.
“Cities and villages in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipro, Rivne, Chernihiv, Mykolaiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions were also hit. In the Sumy region, a railway station came under attack,” the Ukrainian leader added.
Trump held talks with Putin and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, a meeting which was followed by a large “Coalition of the Willing” gathering in Berlin, attended by European leaders as well as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
In a joint statement after the meeting, the group of key Ukrainian allies declared they were ready to join direct negotiations with Moscow, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Russia’s “maximalist demands are not realistic.”
Zelensky on Saturday described the three-way meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi as “very unsuccessful” for the Russian leader, who he said had failed in his goal of trying to recreate a Yalta-style conference at which Allied powers divided up the postwar world in 1945 .
“China did not let itself be drawn in. As for the United States, I don’t know what went on between them and Russia in their bilateral talks, but Ukraine was not discussed. Nothing was said publicly,” Zelensky said in audio messages shared with journalists.
“So, the plan to redraw the world’s borders didn’t work out… I think the summit was a major failure for Russia.”
CNN’s Victoria Butenko and Laura Sharman contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
articles.title_zh: Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials.
"I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference.
Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating.
A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations.
Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO.
"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies."
Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week.
The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries.
Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips.
Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week.
"We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said.
"I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.
The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors.
Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO.
Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.
Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI.
They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.
In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed.
Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.
On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.
Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions."
"I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.
Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show.
Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.
