articles.title_orig: 'They’re blowing this': Amazon's push against NYC delivery worker bill may be backfiring
articles.title_zh: 'They’re blowing this': Amazon's push against NYC delivery worker bill may be backfiring
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
Amazon issued an ultimatum to New Yorkers on Thursday, warning its deliveries would get more expensive if lawmakers pass a bill forcing the company to hire many of its contract delivery workers as regular employees.
People across the five boroughs who opened their Amazon apps to order dish soap or dog treats were greeted by a new banner ad with the word “ATTENTION” bolded and highlighted in red.
“The NYC Council is considering Intro 518, legislation that could increase fees for New Yorkers by up to $5.00 per order,” the ad reads. “This bill would raise costs just when we need to make New York more affordable.”
But the move appears to be backfiring by antagonizing Council Speaker Julie Menin, who could soon bring the measure to a vote.
Menin, a moderate Democrat who is often viewed as an ally of the city’s business class, in recent days grew noticeably frustrated in her public statements as the e-retail giant ramped up its lobbying efforts against the bill, called the Delivery Protection Act .
“Amazon’s campaign is nothing short of a cynical ploy to trick New Yorkers,” Menin said at a press conference Thursday. “It is a last-ditch effort to try to escape the responsibility to the very workers and customers who have made the firm’s success possible.”
Supporters of the bill immediately cried foul.
Amazon used its app to urge New Yorkers to protest the Delivery Protection Act.
“Amazon is a multitrillion-dollar company,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted on social media . “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed.”
“It's a bunch of BS,” said Queens Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the measure’s lead sponsor. “We knew that they were getting desperate.”
The Delivery Protection Act would ban the third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver packages. Although most of the company’s delivery workers wear blue Amazon vests and drive Amazon-branded vans, they work for independent contractors called delivery service partners. There are more than 40 such companies in New York City, according to Amazon, employing about 5,000 people.
Amazon argues the system empowers small businesses and ensures packages are delivered quickly and at low cost. The company points to a study they helped fund that found the Delivery Protection Act would raise costs for customers by about $400 to $660 a year.
“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. The company has threatened to move its warehouses out of New York City if the bill passes.
The banner ad Amazon put out on its app has an “Act Now” button where customers can send emails to city councilmembers. The company said its users sent about 20,000 messages within the first six hours of the campaign launch.
Supporters of the bill argue the measure won’t increase costs for customers, but would improve livelihoods for thousands of delivery workers. Delivery drivers organized by the Teamsters union say the system allows Amazon to escape liability for unsafe work conditions and faulty vehicles. Advocates on the City Council say the bill would force accountability by making Amazon hire its own drivers.
“ There's no world where this common-sense bill would cost Amazon $5 for every single delivery,” Cabán said in an interview. “This is just an example of corporate bullying. They want to bully New Yorkers with junk fees.”
City lobbying data shows the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a group almost entirely funded by Amazon, has spent over $8 million this year opposing the bill.
The scorched-earth PR tactics echo another episode in New York City politics where a tech giant organized its users against proposed legislation.
In 2015, then-Mayor Bill de Blasio and members of the City Council tried to institute a cap limiting the number of for-hire vehicle licenses issued to companies like Uber and Lyft. Uber hired Bradley Tusk , a tech startup PR adviser and investor who managed Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s 2009 re-election campaign, to help sink the proposal.
Tusk describes in his book "The Fixer: My Adventures Saving Startups from Death by Politics," how he flooded the zone with negative TV, radio and digital ads while also ordering his team of lobbyists to “suffocate” individual councilmembers and their staffs. Similar to Amazon issuing a notice to its customers, Uber added a feature in New York known as “de Blasio view” to its app that told users to expect extensive wait times for a car if the legislation passed.
The strategy worked, and de Blasio pulled the bill before a vote. There were about 12,500 vehicles operating for Uber and Lyft in the five boroughs in 2015, according to city data. By 2019, the year lawmakers eventually capped for-hire vehicle licenses, that figure exceeded 86,000. The rapid growth of the e-hailing companies in New York correlated with more traffic congestion and the demise of the city’s yellow taxi industry.
In an interview with Gothamist, Tusk said while Amazon’s strategy may appear similar on the surface, the company was failing to deliver a credible message.
“Nobody believes that Amazon's going to stop delivering in New York,” he said. “So saying, ‘Oh, well, it might be a little more slower,’ or, ‘It might be a little more expensive’ — that doesn't move people.”
Tusk said that Menin could’ve been a sympathetic ear. Instead, he said the negative ads appeared to be driving her closer to politicians to her left, like Mamdani and Cabán, both members of the Democratic Socialists of America.
“Julie is no pushover,” Tusk said. “They’re blowing this.”
While supporters of the Delivery Protection Act like the Teamsters have called for an immediate vote on the bill, Menin has pumped the brakes, saying the legislation needs changes to address legal concerns.
Menin insists the changes won’t weaken the core intent of the bill, but protect it from potential legal challenges. A spokesperson for Cabán’s office said they expect the proposal to come to a vote by the end of the year.
“I have a very clear message for Amazon,” Menin said direct-to-camera during her Thursday press conference. “If you think that that is going to deceive New Yorkers and intimidate the City Council out of passing basic worker and consumer protections, you are dead wrong.”
Walter Wuthmann is a reporter covering public safety and the legal system.

articles.title_zh: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.content_orig:
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. ⁠The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and ⁠pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

articles.title_orig: Is Europe finally ready to play hardball with Putin?
articles.title_zh: Is Europe finally ready to play hardball with Putin?
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, French President Emmanuel Macron, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff pose for a group photo during the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Germany, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
CEO of St. James's Foreign Policy Group
Europe is finally ready to step into negotiations with Russia.
Following this week's meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin , European countries are set to be represented at the negotiating table alongside Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
The continent will be represented by the E5 — Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Poland — together with NATO and the EU representation.
Crucially, they will need to speak with one voice. This is particularly important given the recent dig directed at Europeans by President Trump's son-in-law and chief negotiator Jared Kushner during the talks in Abu Dhabi, where the European representatives were relegated to the sidelines.
The date and format of the next "quad" meeting have yet to be confirmed, but securing Europe's seat at the table is progress, particularly as Russia continues to demand a fundamental redrawing of the European security architecture.
Future negotiations will have to build on the modest achievements of the earlier talks in Saudi Arabia and subsequent diplomatic exchanges of American envoys with the Russians.
Whether Moscow has demonstrated any genuine willingness to compromise is yet to be seen.
The exact outcomes of Steve Witkoff's and Jared Kushner's visit to Moscow on Nov. 12 remain unknown, as do the details of what they have conveyed to President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. But just hearing the snippets of the meeting in the Kremlin that have almost certainly been deliberately made public makes it clear that Putin has not moved an inch away from his maximalist demands.
The set of demands made during the Istanbul negotiations in March 2022 remains unchanged: no foreign troops, the disarmament of Ukraine, neutral status and full exposure to Russian occupation with no external interference.
In November 2026, the negotiations have come full circle.
It's not surprising that Zelensky insists that Russia is not ready for peace. Moreover, as the Russian saying goes, "the appetite comes during the meal."
One can argue that Putin did not just return to his demands from the first months of the invasion; he went back to the ones he made to former U.S. President Joe Biden in 2021.
Putting the issue of "European security architecture" on the negotiating table — especially as Europeans themselves are not at said table — only proves the point Ukraine has been trying to make for almost five years of full-scale invasion: if you don't stop Putin in Ukraine, he will go for Europe.
Undoubtedly, it is Europe's strong resolve to support Ukraine, while the United States has stepped back from providing military and financial aid, that has caused an allergic reaction in the Kremlin.
Moreover, Europe's newfound determination to enhance its own defense and deterrence capabilities has sent Russia a strong signal —  and, importantly, it's time for Europe to accelerate, not stop right now.
“We are back in the world of predators.”
Many important steps have already been taken: Europe is no longer critically dependent on Russian oil and gas, nor is it willing to put business ahead of its security.
Having witnessed Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine for almost five years, and faced with uncertainty over the once unquestionably reliable transatlantic alliance, the EU has made a fundamental shift — from being primarily an economic community to one with a geopolitical agency and defense readiness as one of its key priorities.
"We are back in the world of predators," as the former long-serving Secretary-General of the European Parliament and now advisor to the EU Defense Commissioner, Klaus Welle, put it. Europe has realized that it needs to become stronger to survive in this world.
Brussels has started actively discussing the future of European security architecture with Ukraine at its center, and ways to operationalize Article 42.7 of the Treaty on European Union – the EU's own mutual assistance clause similar to NATO 's Article 5.
It has also boosted its defense spending in the Multiannual Financial Framework, established a dedicated Security and Defense Committee in the European Parliament , and is trying to better align national defense industries to enhance interoperability, thus translating industrial capacity into joint capability planning.
Separately, to move away from a paralyzing veto power and towards a qualified majority vote in decision-making (think Hungary), Europe is looking towards creating a brand new intergovernmental arrangement parallel to the EU, like a European Defense Union with a European Security Council as its governing body.
Ukraine is being discussed as one of its most critical members who will be shaping a new military doctrine for the European pillar of NATO.
Naturally, these gradual but unprecedented moves in the EU have ruffled some feathers in the Kremlin, prompting it to put the issue of the European security architecture up for discussion.
The Europeans, realizing that they must reestablish their agency in securing an acceptable end to the war on their continent, are now seeking broader representation in negotiations with Russia.
The fact that the EU has now taken on a greater share of financial support for Ukraine gives it a valid argument with the Americans, and $300 billion in Russian sovereign assets held in Belgium adds some leverage over Russians.
There are even talks about appointing a permanent EU envoy to Russia. A clear mandate for the position, as well as the candidacy itself, has not been drawn up yet, with many names being thrown in the ring, but the willingness to take more initiative is reassuring.
Europe should get involved in ceasefire negotiations in Ukraine, as it will be European troops observing that ceasefire.
British, French, and other European troops have been preparing for that mission, including through exercises in Poland. But even more so, Ukraine has now become an indispensable part of the European community.
This realization has finally become irreversible, not just in Kyiv but also in Brussels.
As Ukraine progresses towards its formal accession to the EU , many talks in Brussels focus on how to bring Ukraine closer sooner.
"Ukraine’s perception is shifting from being a recipient of aid to the continent’s net security provider."
There have been several attempts to float the idea of associate membership, which understandably caused a painful reaction in Ukraine, with fears of being trumped — in all the new senses of the word — but behind closed doors European officials are reassuring that this, on the contrary, is a way to bring the country at war into European structures sooner.
Others are suggesting replacing the word "associate" with "progressive" membership.
Such wordplay may seem negligible to the outsider, but within the EU corridors they can significantly shift the dynamic for an aspiring member.
Regardless, Ukraine's perception is shifting from being a recipient of aid to the continent's net security provider.
Europe has now accepted the fact that the best chance it has for strategic self-sufficiency in defense is by building on Ukraine's acquired battlefield experience and defense innovation.
Naturally, Ukrainian drone innovation takes center stage, but perhaps even more valuable is the new military doctrine taking shape in Ukraine. It is not only about cheaper, more agile hardware but the smart and sophisticated ways of deploying it — a panoply of terrain navigation, electronic warfare, the application of AI-driven C4ISR, anticipation of Russia's next move, and denial of action — ultimately, the most successful operationalization of data on the battlefield in modern history.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s latest flight of fancy involves potentially launching billions of dollars worth of cutting-edge AI chips into space.
Starting in late 2025 , the world’s richest man began pushing the ludicrous idea of launching AI data centers into orbit. Though humanity remains decades — if not centuries — away from cracking the physics on that fantastical concept, Musk has only become more enamored by the idea with the success of SpaceX’s debut on the public market.
Should he ever choose to pull the trigger on his orbital data centers, Musk would undoubtedly draw on the company’s incoming collection of Nvidia chips, financed by a massive loan from a cohort of the world’s most powerful banks.
The banks depending on those chips as collateral for SpaceX’s debt, however, are rightfully mortified.
New reporting by the Financial Times revealed that lenders backing a $43 billion SpaceX debt package — secured by the company’s cache of physical AI chips — have been trying to block any attempt by Musk and his board to greenlight a chip launch.
Given the fact that nobody has ever even attempted such a feat, SpaceX lenders would basically view any chips blasted into the stratosphere as lost, anonymous insiders told the FT . It’s not hard to see why: even if the chips do make it safely into orbit, physically repossessing them in the event that SpaceX defaults on its $43 billion loan would be a logistical nightmare.
While the contents of the final debt arrangement led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs are unknown to the public, the FT notes that an earlier proposal contained language allowing banks to legally challenge Musk’s orbital ambitions.
On a technical level, space-bound data centers are an absurdity at best. Each satellite would require enormous solar panel arrays to power low-gravity cooling pumps needed to dissipate heat, and if anything goes wrong, they’re a planet away from the nearest IT technician. That’s to say nothing of the regulatory hurdles around beaming that much data back and forth, or the impacts of solar radiation .

articles.title_orig: Estonia-Russia border closure sparks residents' rush to cross
articles.title_zh: Estonia-Russia border closure sparks residents' rush to cross
articles.content_orig:
People carrying suitcases, backpacks and plastic bags have been gathering in the Russian border town of Ivangorod, hoping to cross into Estonia before the Baltic country closes its land border with Russia next month.
The queues reflect the impact of a decision that will affect not only cross-border travel but also families with relatives living on opposite sides of the frontier.
Estonia, a member of NATO and the European Union, announced on 20 November that it would suspend road crossings at all five road border checkpoints with Russia from 1 December. The restriction is due to remain in place for six months, after which the government will review the security situation and decide whether to extend or amend it.
The decision follows an attempted arson attack on the premises of Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, on 14 November.
According to Estonia's Internal Security Service, Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was behind the attempted attack. Eight Latvian citizens were detained, with investigators suspecting they had been recruited to carry out the operation. The company's security staff intervened before significant damage was caused.
Estonian authorities described the incident as part of a wider pattern of sabotage (source in Estonian) and hostile activity against the country and other European states. The government said the border closure would make it harder for Russian intelligence services to recruit and influence people crossing into Estonia, as well as help prevent sanctions evasion.
Moscow has rejected the accusations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the allegations as unfounded, while Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Estonia of infringing the rights of Russian citizens and threatened political and diplomatic countermeasures.
Zakharova also compared the planned closure to the construction of a new Iron Curtain.
For people living in the border region, the decision has consequences extending far beyond security policy.
Narva, an Estonian town of more than 50,000 people, lies directly opposite Ivangorod on the other side of the River Narva. The two towns have long-standing family, social and economic ties, with many residents having relatives on both sides.
The crossing has also been used by people travelling from other European countries to reach St Petersburg.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through the Narva crossing in February 2024, but pedestrians have continued to cross.
Narva Mayor Jaan Toots has called on the Estonian government to consider humanitarian exemptions for residents who need to visit elderly relatives, attend funerals or deal with other urgent family matters. He has also warned of economic consequences for the town, including potential losses for local hotels, restaurants and businesses.
The closure is also expected to affect employment in the region, where border guards and customs officers are among the local workforce.
The number of people travelling between Estonia and Russia has declined considerably since the start of the war in Ukraine.
According to Estonian public broadcaster ERR, annual crossings fell from more than four million before 2022 to around 760,000 in 2026. Of those, approximately 447,000 were made through the Narva-Ivangorod crossing, according to the figures cited by AFP.
Reuters reported that Russian nationals accounted for 307,000 of this year's crossings, while 175,000 were made by Estonian citizens and 54,000 by Finnish passport holders.
The planned restrictions will apply to all five road crossing points: Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. Rail freight will continue, subject to existing restrictions and customs checks.
Travellers will have to use alternative routes through neighbouring countries, particularly Latvia, although journeys are likely to become longer and more expensive.
For those without access to a car, travelling by air may become the only practical alternative.
The closure is currently planned for six months, rather than indefinitely. Estonia's government says it will reassess the measure after that period, depending on the security situation.

articles.title_orig: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.title_zh: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.content_orig:
A survey of AI proxy services suggests stablecoins have become a key payment rail for Chinese users accessing restricted US models
Sat 21 Nov 2026 · 10:35 EST · 2 min read
Every time a major US AI lab ships a new frontier model, a shadow market on the other side of the Pacific starts paying up. In stablecoins.
That is the core finding of a new report from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. It found that payments from wallets suspected of links to China jumped 55% above baseline within three days of key US AI model releases.
Export controls were meant to keep advanced American AI out of reach. Instead, they appear to have created demand for a middleman economy, and crypto is helping settle the bill.
The report, published on November 21, 2026, describes a market where Chinese users reach restricted US frontier AI models through proxy or agent services. These services act as go-betweens, offering access that export controls would otherwise block.
Chainalysis surveyed 100 of these service providers. Of those, 40% accept payment in crypto, with stablecoins doing most of the work.
The timing pattern is what makes the data stand out. Activity from suspected China-linked wallets did not just drift upward over time. It spiked right after new US models dropped, which Chainalysis read as a sign of a coordinated rush to tap the latest capabilities.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
Chainalysis described an ecosystem with increasingly specialized roles.
Access suppliers provide the underlying connection to US models. Brokers connect buyers to that access. Payment processors handle the money side of the transaction.
Some of those payment players go a step further. According to the report, certain processors obscure stablecoin transactions by routing them through third-party channels, making the trail harder to follow.
The economics help explain why. Chainalysis noted that paying for proxy access is cheaper than training comparable models from scratch. Users can query US models and distill those capabilities into local systems, essentially learning from the output rather than building the foundation themselves.
The AI findings build on earlier Chainalysis work. A report released in October 2026 had already flagged a significant rise in peer-to-peer stablecoin transactions from China-linked wallets, despite domestic restrictions on crypto trading.
That October report recorded $104.1 billion in self-custodied stablecoin transfers from China-linked wallets. Those transfers came across 18.1 million transactions between July 2025 and June 2026.
Over the past year, the Chinese crypto ecosystem has been estimated at at least $176 billion. Peer-to-peer activity accounted for 59.1% of that total.

articles.title_orig: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
articles.title_zh: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
articles.content_orig:
As Jensen Huang games out a possible return to Nvidia as CEO, the 63-year-old chip mogul is turning to a pocket-sized lifeline: his phone.
On the other end of the line are a series of tech CEOs, Nvidia employees, and President Donald Trump, who are offering kind words and positing avenues by which he could return to the helm .
"I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," venture capitalist Gavin Baker said recently in an interview on CNBC. "I think he has more to contribute to America, to AI, and technology."
Huang resigned on November 12 in the wake of accusations that he had at least two affairs, one with a Chinese executive that US intelligence says is spying for Beijing and another with a direct report at Nvidia. Huang has since indicated an interest in returning as CEO.
In a lengthy X post five days after he resigned, Huang said he's seen an "outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO."
"Many continue to reach out to me directly," he added.
Nvidia's board, however, has said that it has no plans to reinstate the founder, who wrote in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, Lori Huang.
Here's what some influential people say they told Huang.
Trump says he called Jensen Huang at least twice since news of his affairs broke.
In a White House press conference three days before Huang resigned, Trump said he'd called Huang that day "just to see if he's feeling all right."
Trump said he asked Huang whether he knew that Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of Megaspeed and his alleged paramour, was a spy for China. Trump said Huang said he didn't know.
Then, in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, Trump said Huang called him at a separate time, telling the president that he feels bad for what he's done to his family.
The New York Times reported that in one of those calls, Trump urged Huang to fight to keep his job.
Travis Kalanick, the former CEO of Uber who now heads an AI robotics firm called Atoms, said he wrote Huang with an auspicious promise.
"I will show up to Nvidia HQ with a wafer-encrusted megaphone, with tons of Nvidia employees who want to walk out, tons of CEOs, founders," he said recently at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin.
Kalanick resigned from Uber in 2017 under pressure following an investigation into its workplace culture. He said he told Huang that a petition for a CEO's return was good, but a walkout was better.
"Let's fight for what's right," Kalanick said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he's spoken with Jensen Huang since the scandal.
"It's hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen," Altman said at The New York Times DealBook summit.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman, sitting beside Altman, said he and his wife are friends with Huang's family. He said he reached out "just to be there for him."
Asked whether Huang thinks he can return as CEO, Altman said: "Greg and I have like a little more empathy toward the situation than the average person."
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he texted Huang to let the Nvidia founder know he is thinking of him.
"I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next," Nadella said at a media roundtable on November 17.
At the DealBook summit, Nadella called the situation "pretty tragic."
Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said his "most consistent message" to Huang has been to work out and maintain healthy habits.
"I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," Baker said on CNBC. "Because to be a sound mind, he needs to be a sound body."
Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at the hedge fund Atreides Management, said he considers Huang a friend and added that Huang has more to contribute to AI.

articles.title_orig: Honda, Toyota Recall 1.6M Vehicles Over Airbag Risk
articles.title_zh: Honda, Toyota Recall 1.6M Vehicles Over Airbag Risk
articles.content_orig:
Toyota is recalling 314,029 Toyota and Lexus vehicles in the United States over passenger airbag inflators that could rupture, sending metal fragments toward occupants and risking serious injury or death.
Toyota is recalling more than 314,000 vehicles in the U.S. because front passenger airbag inflators made by Takata could rupture and hurl metal fragments at occupants, increasing the risk of serious injury or death.
The recall affects 314,029 Toyota and Lexus vehicles from the 2002 through 2017 model years, according to a report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and reported by Reuters.
Affected models include the Toyota Corolla, Tundra, Sequoia and 4Runner, along with the Lexus SC430, IS250 and GX460.
FORD RECALLS 60,000 TRANSIT VANS OVER SOFTWARE GLITCH THAT SHUTS OFF LIGHTS
Certain Toyota 4Runner sport utility vehicles are included in Toyota's recall of 314,029 U.S. vehicles over Takata front passenger airbag inflators that may rupture. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Toyota reported no ruptures involving the affected inflators, according to the NHTSA recall report.
The problem stems from Takata front passenger airbag inflators that are nearing the end of their estimated safe service life. NHTSA said the inflators could rupture due to propellant degradation after long-term exposure to high humidity, high temperatures and high temperature cycling.
If the front passenger airbag deploys in a crash, the degraded inflator could rupture and send sharp metal fragments into the cabin.
POPULAR TIRE BRAND RECALLS TIRES OVER HIDDEN DEFECT THAT COULD CAUSE A SUDDEN CRASH WHILE DRIVING
Toyota Motor Corp's logo at a dealership in Tokyo, Japan, April 3, 2025. (Kim Kyung-Hoon/Reuters / Reuters)
Toyota said it is conducting the recall out of an abundance of caution, according to NHTSA.
Depending on the vehicle , authorized Toyota and Lexus dealers will replace the front passenger airbag inflator or the entire airbag assembly free of charge, the agency said.
Owners can check whether their vehicles are included in the recall by visiting NHTSA's recall database at nhtsa.gov/recalls and entering a 17-digit vehicle identification number or by contacting an authorized Toyota or Lexus dealership.
Toyota plans to mail owner notification letters between Dec. 28 and Jan. 11, according to the NHTSA filing, though owners do not have to wait for those letters to contact a dealer about repairs.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 PS5 Review Bombing Out of Control as Zelda Receives Revenge Ratings
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 PS5 Review Bombing Out of Control as Zelda Receives Revenge Ratings
articles.content_orig:
Update [ Sat 21st Nov 2026, 3:30pm ]:
In response to a coordinated review bombing effort on GTA 6 , fans of the Rockstar release appear to have launched a counter-attack on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time , believing Nintendo gamers are to blame for the situation.
Last night, I reported that GTA 6’s Metacritic user score was racking up ‘0’ review scores at an unprecedented pace. Many of the ratings were bogus.
In the hours since, the Switch 2’s universally adored remake of Ocarina of Time has seen its user score drop from 9.6 to 8.9 at the time of writing.
One ‘0’ rating simply reads: “Take your own medicine.”
At this point, I just wish Metacritic would do away with user scores, although I’ve no doubt this sorry situation is all good for business.
The thing is: this isn’t the first time the critic aggregator has become a battleground like this. As I mentioned in my original report, many of the greatest games ever made have pitiful user scores on the site.
Hopefully this all blows over, because it’s all rather embarrassing right now.
Original Story: GTA 6 , the highest-rated game of all-time , is getting review bombed on Metacritic as idiots attempt to plunge the seminal Rockstar release’s rating with bogus ‘0’ scores.
At the time of writing, the title has a user score of 5.4 , meaning it’s considered ‘Mixed or Average’:
This is in sharp contrast to critics, who awarded the game an average score of 99, making it the best-reviewed title of all time.
“Good thing Rockstar doesn’t blacklist user ratings like they do critics,” one review reads.
There’s a theory among some online that the dev blacklists media outlets for giving its games poor scores, but it put GTA 6 in the hands of more than 150 critics, so I don’t buy that for a single second.
Many of the ‘0’ reviews all touch on the same thing: 30fps is “unplayable”, the series has gone “woke”, and the “story is horrible”. (“I never smiled one time,” writes one seemingly perpetually miserable user.)
There are some legitimate criticisms among these; one person writes they’re not a fan of the life sim elements and prefer the “power fantasy” of older games. That’s fair, but it doesn’t make it a ‘0’.
Metacritic reviews have always been a disaster really, because you don’t need to actually own a game to rate it. Many of the best titles ever released have dreadful user scores on the site.
On the PS Store , though – where you actually have to spend money on the game to score it – the current rating sits at 4.84 based on 170k reviews. So that’s probably a better reflection of how the community feels.
My take on all this is that humans are predictable creatures: wherever there’s something popular, you’re probably going to find a group of people eager to tear it down.

articles.title_orig: Modders Are Trying to Create a PC Native Version of GTA 6 With Its Leaked Xbox Series X Build
articles.title_zh: Modders Are Trying to Create a PC Native Version of GTA 6 With Its Leaked Xbox Series X Build
articles.content_orig:
Just when it seemed Cyberleek had disappeared for good, the notorious leaker has returned. Even though the GTA 6 release date has passed, the individual has followed through on past threats. A decrypted Xbox build is spreading through piracy networks, which could lead to a playable PC port . However, there is one major caveat with the 209 GB download.
The Cyberleek website now displays a message about the latest leak. While prior gameplay videos appeared to be from a PC-based development build , they elected to distribute GTA 6 Xbox files. Allegedly, this version is from November 2026, and images of a file structure exposing assets have emerged. Regardless, it may have limited use without the missing executable file.
Once again, Cyberleek hopes to raise cryptocurrency funds before releasing the critical file. Offering a playable build as the reward, they previously set a $30 million market capitalization goal for a meme coin. That October initiative failed, but hitting the $15 million mark will supposedly unlock the .exe.
Notably, a timer is also counting down from under 4 days. Once it expires, Rockstar ’s tormentor promises to circulate the executable on piracy sites anyway.
It's unclear how soon the GTA 6 Xbox files may result in a bootable game for PC users. Cyberleek believes hackers will find a way to emulate the console version for Windows within a week. As criticism of the 30 fps performance target continues, capable hardware could produce higher frame rates.
Unfortunately for pirates, no working Series X emulator currently exists. The hardware found in the Microsoft console and many PCs is similar, with CPUs sharing x86-64 architecture. Still, among other challenges, the Series X runs a custom OS that would need to be adapted for a Windows environment.
Another possibility is a decompilation project targeting the leaked GTA 6 Xbox files. Developers would analyze, modify, and reconstruct the code into a version that can boot on PCs.
Cyberleek also claims to possess a PS5 build as a fallback option. Besides accumulating cryptocurrency, the objective is to prevent console and PC ports from doubling Take-Two and Rockstar's profits.

articles.title_orig: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.title_zh: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.content_orig:
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as UN-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
Scores of countries ended the weeklong UN conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn’t commit to binding rules sought by UN Secretary-General António Guterres , many countries and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts as major military powers jockey for dominance.
It also marked the latest failure to set guardrails for AI, at a time when some experts have warned about such systems breaking out of human control and going rogue.
Izumi Nakamitsu, the UN high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.
Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounted to “pushing the can down the road for two more years.”
They noted that most countries supported work toward a new treaty.
Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: “States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities.”
Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.
“Technology is moving faster than diplomacy,” said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. “Diplomats are very slow.”
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, had set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
The UN’s Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday and “start thinking about how to get as strong as possible instrument to prohibit and regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems.”
The International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted how autonomous weapons can be “unpredictable” — unlike, say, a bullet fired from a gun with a distinct and predictable trajectory.
“For years, the ICRC and many others have urged states to ensure that humans retain control over the use of force and that life-and-death decisions are never handed over to machines,” it said in a statement.
Advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism at this week’s talks largely by Russia, which, like other leading developers of AI weapons, including the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Pope Leo XIV and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate , urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.
Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and any deal is likely to be based on the lowest common denominator.

articles.title_orig: The Fastest Way To Increase Focus Levels In ‘GTA 6’
articles.title_zh: The Fastest Way To Increase Focus Levels In ‘GTA 6’
articles.content_orig:
First introduced back in GTA 5 alongside Red Dead's Deadeye system, Focus Mode is back for both Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI , with a few cool upgrades. This official IGN GTA 6 guide teaches you how Focus works, including while in and out of combat, when pinpointing the source of a noise, and when tracking vehicles and animals.
Click on a link below to jump to that specific section of this guide:
Unlike in GTA 5 where Franklin, Michael, and Trevor each had their own unique special abilities, Focus Mode works the same way for both main characters in GTA 6 and feels a lot like Michael's classic bullet-time ability.
You can trigger Focus Mode by clicking in both sticks ( Left Stick Click + Right Stick Click / Left Stick Click + Right Stick Click ) the same time , though how it works changes slightly depending on whether you’re actively in combat or not.
Enabling Focus slows down time and highlights interactive objects around you. If you aren't actively aiming down sights or shooting, Focus Mode won't drain your meter at all – even when you're behind the wheel.
When you aren't aiming, Focus Mode helps you spot openable doors, color-coded loot, and bad guys. It lasts for 30 seconds when on foot and has a two-second cooldown once the 30-second limit has been exhausted. That said, you can reactivate it immediately if you haven’t drained the full 30 seconds.
When you use Focus while driving, you get extra breathing room to pull off tricky driving maneuvers. It won't boost your vehicle's handling like Franklin's ability used to in GTA 5, but the extra reaction time makes a huge difference when you're dodging cops or rival gangs. Plus, police officers glow blue, making them easy to spot and avoid in areas where you are wanted.
Focus Mode lasts for 30 seconds when driving, though this is affected by speed: the faster you go, the less time you get in Focus Mode. It can drop to as low as 10 seconds if you’re driving super fast. It also has a two-second cooldown between uses. Everything interactive is color-coded while Focus Mode is active:
You'll also see weapons lying on the ground highlighted in red, so you can grab them easily.
Your meter drains if you aim when using Focus in combat - this is called Combat Focus . When you line up a shot on an enemy, you'll see yellow and red target spots appear on their body as the meter depletes.
Yellow spots indicate limbs where shots will wound or disarm them – aiming for a hand can make them drop their gun, while hitting a leg can knock them down. Red spots mark lethal target areas on the head and heart for quick kills. Target hotspots aren't just for enemies; they show up on vehicles too. For land vehicles, aim for the tires or engine block to quickly disable them. If you're dealing with helicopters, target the engine or rotor assemblies to bring them down.
Keep in mind that aiming in Combat Focus burns through your meter fast. A quick way to refill your meter when you're out of combat is to smoke a cigarette. Additionally, if Jason/Lucia’s Criminal Profile is Professional, incapacitations boosts your meter. If their Criminal Profile is Violent or worse, landing headshots increases it instead.
Another main use for Focus Mode while out in the world is to use it to find noises. Often, an event can be happening close by, but you may not be able to tell exactly where it is coming from. Focus Mode will show sound ripples in the air, pointing you directly to the action. This is incredibly useful for scoping out Side Missions and activities, as it will help tell the difference between an NPC just talking to someone else or the start of an activity or Side Mission. These ripples will also appear for any police cars, K9 dogs, and helicopters that are actively searching for you while you’re Wanted, plus any witnesses to the crime.
Tracking returns in GTA 6, and Focus is the way to do it! When chasing down a vehicle during a mission, using Focus will show their trails, allowing you to keep up with where they are heading. Similarly, the animal tracking mechanic returns from Red Dead Redemption 2. When hunting for wildlife, entering Focus Mode will show you scent trails for various creatures, going so far as to inform you what animal is making the scent.
Luckily, you don’t need to stay locked into Focus when tracking wildlife, as there’s a prompt to track a specific animal and it will stay on your screen even after exiting Focus Mode.

An Israeli strike killed three Palestinians in a vehicle carrying papers and food for ⁠the World Central Kitchen charity in Gaza City on Saturday, Gaza's health ministry and witnesses said.
World Central Kitchen, an aid organisation that distributes food in the Gaza Strip, said, however, that the vehicle was not affiliated with it.
The Israeli military said several militants had been targeted in the area without providing further ⁠details. It did not immediately respond to questions ​on ⁠why it had hit a vehicle that appeared to be distributing aid.
A witness said the vehicle appeared to be carrying packaged foodstuffs, and that papers inside ⁠carried World Central Kitchen's logo.
"It was just about to stop to distribute the food ​and drink to ⁠children when it was hit ‌by a missile," said Abu Zein Al-Daya, who witnessed the strike.
Afterwards, meals of cooked rice were scattered around the vehicle, which was partially covered in the blood of the victims of ‌the attack.
The Israeli military killed ‌seven World Central Kitchen workers in a 2024 strike, including citizens of Australia, Britain and Poland.
At the time, the military said there had been "serious errors and breaches of procedure" but in 2026 it said it had found no ⁠basis on which to open criminal investigations into the incident.
Israel briefly launched a ground operation in Gaza earlier this week and killed six people in a strike on a hospital that it said was targeting a commander for the Palestinian militant group Hamas .
An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory but has not stopped Israeli attacks on Gaza or secured Hamas' disarmament.
At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since then, ‌according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.
Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of ​Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with ‌Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along ⁠Gaza's coast.
Israel's more than two-year-long assault on Gaza has killed tens of thousands, ⁠caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and a United ‌Nations inquiry.
Israel says its ​actions are self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 ‌people and took more than 250 hostages ​in an October 2023 attack on Israel.

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI PS5 Streams/Captures Get DLSS 5 and Frame Generation on PC Through Veyra/Neural Screen, But Gameplay Still Runs at 30FPS (with More Latency)
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI PS5 Streams/Captures Get DLSS 5 and Frame Generation on PC Through Veyra/Neural Screen, But Gameplay Still Runs at 30FPS (with More Latency)
articles.content_orig:
We started playing Grand Theft Auto VI on a workbench with a processor AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card. A PlayStation 5 Pro console was connected to the computer via an AVerMedia Live Gamer ULTRA 2.1 GC553G2 external video capture card, and the game was run at 4K resolution with maximum graphics settings. Image output was organized using OBS Studio, and video recording was done using the NVIDIA App. To transform the image and achieve maximum smoothness, we enabled NVIDIA DLSS 5 (3D-Guided Neural Rendering) real-time generative neural rendering with the Natural profile and DLSS 4.5 frame generation in 6X mode using NeuralScreen v2.6.4.
In the opening scene in a correctional facility featuring protagonist Lucia Caminos, we directly compared standard console graphics and neural rendering. NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology works on top of the standard image to add photorealistic visual effects, radically changing the perception of the scene. With the neural network enabled, Lucia's face, skin texture, strands of hair, the folds of her prison uniform, and the soft light falling from the window all became realistically rendered. Simultaneously, six-times frame generation boosted performance to stable 262 and 280 FPS, with peaks of 286 FPS, ensuring incredibly smooth movement.
The RTX 5090 graphics card utilized 62% to 75% of its system capacity while running DLSS 5 generative neural rendering, maintaining a core clock of 2857 to 2917 MHz at temperatures ranging from 57° to 65°C and power consumption ranging from 305W to 368W. Without active neural rendering, with frame generation only, the GPU utilization dropped to 37% and 40%, while power consumption dropped to 189W and 214W. The system utilized approximately 5,3GB of video memory, and just over 12GB of RAM. AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D It ran stably at 5225 MHz, with temperatures ranging from 57° to 63° C and power consumption ranging from 41W to 48W, handling real-time streaming of Grand Theft Auto VI without issue.

articles.title_orig: PS5 Survives GTA 6's Unfathomably Humongous Launch without a Hitch
articles.title_zh: PS5 Survives GTA 6's Unfathomably Humongous Launch without a Hitch
articles.content_orig:
Sony has confirmed that the recently released PS5 firmware 14.23 update is required to play GTA 6, in a social media post boosted by Rockstar Games.
Yesterday November 17, Sony released PS5 system software update 26.07-14.23.00 , which weighed in at 1.267 GB. According to Sony’s official patch notes, it makes “some security fixes to the system software.”
Now, just hours before GTA 6 launches at midnight across the world, the PlayStation Support U.S. X / Twitter account confirmed what many had suspected: “Sony Interactive has issued a PS5 system software update that is required before playing Grand Theft Auto VI. Players should download this update prior to midnight on November 19 so that they’re ready to play on launch day, November 19.” The official Rockstar Games account then reposted it to its 23.7 million followers.
It is believed this unprecedented PS5 update cuts PlayStation Network access to older firmware, which means if you haven’t upgraded to 14.23 you will not be able to play GTA 6 on PS5. 14.23 released just a day after a prominent PS5 hacker claimed to be the first person to have “dumped” a game binary at 14.22, although they did not share any jailbreak.
The PlayStation homebrew scene has made headlines in the last two months for releasing PS5 jailbreaks for prior firmwares. For example, late September, a jailbreak that supported all PS5 consoles running firmware 7.00-13.60 sent shockwaves through the homebrew community because, at the time, it meant that all PS5s, including the PS5 Pro, that hadn't been updated within the previous week were compatible with the jailbreak. This was of huge significance for Sony and the security of the PS5, as people with a jailbroken PS5 can modify their console, potentially opening the door to video game piracy.
However, it was found that some PS5 games subsequently required the more recent 14.00 firmware in order to download updates, sparking a renewed effort to release a new jailbreak for the updated system software. So, there is a game of Whac-A-Mole at play where the homebrew scene is working to release a new jailbreak for the latest PS5 firmware, then do it all over again when Sony releases a new firmware update designed to beef up security.
This in turn has sparked concern that if a PS5 jailbreak was made available for the firmware that is required by GTA 6, then it may be possible for Rockstar’s game to be pirated on PS5 and maybe even made available on PC.
The question for Sony is whether it can do enough to eventually win this game of Whac-A-Mole with the homebrew scene. This is something of an existential crisis for Sony, which publishers and developers rely upon for the security of their PlayStation releases. But with the emergence of powerful AI models, the stakes have risen significantly.
Just last week, Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two, told IGN that the company was taking security seriously , and insisted that fans will prefer to play GTA 6 officially, with all its bells and whistles as Rockstar intended, over an unofficial PC version.
During an investor-focused Q&A, Zelnick was asked multiple times about this AI reverse-engineering problem. He, again, had strong words in response, suggesting Take-Two was ready to lawyer up.
“This business has been largely immune to piracy concerns forever because of file sizes, complexity of piracy, being connected to servers and the like,” he began. “And undoubtedly, it would be very difficult to replicate the experience of consuming our game as intended because of technical limitations.
“That said, it's going to become more of a challenge, as you said, and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it.”
GTA 6 is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, and some companies have even given staff bonus time off to play it . We've got plenty more on GTA 6 ahead of its November 19 launch, including details on the New Zealand trick people are using to play early, Gangland Tales From the Frontline of Rockstar's Real-Life Grand Theft Auto Research , and — finally — confirmation of the actress who plays Lucia .

articles.title_orig: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
articles.title_zh: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
articles.content_orig:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
after newsletter promotion
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

articles.title_orig: Many Etsy Sellers Close Up Shop Over Site’s New A.I. Policy
articles.title_zh: Many Etsy Sellers Close Up Shop Over Site’s New A.I. Policy
articles.content_orig:
Sign up to get our news digest — delivered directly to your inbox twice a week.
Following a hugely unpopular update to Etsy’s terms of use, artists are shutting down their shops in droves and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next.
The reason is right there in the online market’s updated terms. Starting December 16, the agreement explicitly gives Etsy and its third-party partners and vendors permission to use content uploaded by sellers to train and improve AI systems.
Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers.
Etsy says it uses sellers’ content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn’t train models designed to copy artists’ work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content.
A post shared by Aaron Millard (@aaronmillardillustration)
A post shared by Cognitive Surplus (@cognitivesurplus)
A post shared by aaron meshon (@aaronmeshon)
A post shared by Leanne (@snackhungrycreations)
A post shared by Cognitive Surplus (@cognitivesurplus)
For an independent animator, an Etsy shop can bring in money between gigs by selling character stickers, prints from a short, or zines of development art. It’s also a popular platform for merch sales that can help finance original projects.
Closing a shop just weeks before the holidays means giving up potential sales, years of reviews, and a storefront customers already know how to find. The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it’s worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI.
Etsy will surely continue to run its site and fill the search results with more prints, stickers, and custom pet portraits than anyone could ever scroll through. But when the artists who made the marketplace worth visiting are telling customers where to find them next, why keep sifting through the slop?

articles.title_orig: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
articles.title_zh: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
articles.content_orig:
Frankhoermann/Sven Simon/DPA/Zuma
A Missouri judge on Friday granted final approval to Bayer’s $7.25 billion settlement of class action lawsuits that claimed its weedkiller, Roundup, causes cancer. The settlement, which is subject to appeal, was “designed to resolve current and future” claims, Bayer representatives wrote in a press release, and close the courthouse doors to anyone else seeking restitution over the herbicide from the $50 billion company. “Monsanto pursued the class settlement to significantly contain the litigation, and the settlement agreement does not contain any admission of liability or wrongdoing,” they wrote.
The $7.25 billion settlement may shake out to relatively small amounts of money per individual plaintiff—somewhere between $10,000 and $100,000 per person. Nonetheless, Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed lawyer for cancer patients in the case, claimed victory. “Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” he said.
When Bayer bought weedkiller manufacturer Monsanto in 2018, the German company inherited approximately 65,000 lawsuits filed against Monsanto over the past decade. Most of those suits alleged that the company’s weedkiller—which contains the controversial chemical glyphosate—caused people to develop cancers like non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.
Vast numbers of people say they were harmed by the company, and members of the Make America Healthy Again movement have pressured the federal government to crack down on glyphosate. Still, Bayer has slowly but surely won a string of court cases. Much of the litigation was settled through a $10 billion settlement in 2020; five months ago, the Supreme Court ruled in a landmark case that the company could not be held liable for causing a man to develop cancer. That ruling, notably, was based on a 2013 study that was “ghost written” by Monsanto itself , and deemed compromised by the Environmental Protection Agency.
The company has put significant resources into shaping public opinion of glyphosate: In December of 2025, another influential journal article from 2000 that found glyphosate to be safe was retracted after its editor announced the authors had not disclosed Monsanto’s role in writing the paper. A recent Mother Jones investigation about glyphosate spraying in national forests found other examples of Monsanto’s hand in secretly orchestrating research papers.
Nonetheless, Friday’s settlement means suing the company will be more difficult in the future. “The Court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement .
Dan Friedman and Russ Choma

articles.title_orig: Economists Are Hyperventilating Over the AI Bubble
articles.title_zh: Economists Are Hyperventilating Over the AI Bubble
articles.content_orig:
Don’t panic about the AI bubble, folks — just ignore all the economists hyperventilating about it in the corner.
The absurdly swift rise of Anthropic has experts feeling baffled and gloomy about the future of Wall Street. Becoming a $1.5 trillion dollar company, after its blockbuster IPO finalized Wednesday, in just a matter of years is unprecedented, signaling that AI is sending our economy into yet more unprecedented territory. And that uncertainty is scary.
“No company in history has grown so big, so fast,” David B. Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor, told the Washington Post .
And the pressure is on, he added: “Expectations for continued rapid growth will be off the charts.”
Talk of a bubble has loomed over the industry for years, but investors have been antsier of late. More than ever, they fear that the trillions being poured into AI won’t lead to a return on investment in the near future. Google’s market cap plummeted by half a trillion dollars in a day last month, WaPo noted, after its earnings showed that its chief source of revenue, search advertising, was growing more slowly than predicted because of its difficulty monetizing its AI search features that are also pushing users away from seeing traditional search ads.
The most promising avenue for AI making money was through enterprise sales. Corporate customers and businesses were happily paying for access to frontier coding tools from major labs like Anthropic. But many customers have since been rattled by the often exorbitant costs of using these AI tools — one immortal example: a company that reportedly blew $500 million on Claude tokens in a single month — and have placed tighter spending limits or adopted a hybrid approach of using a mix of cheaper Chinese models as an alternative.
There’s also been the sort of fantasy-land salesmanship characteristic of the hubris an industry exudes before the bubble inevitably bursts. This summer, SpaceX rebranded itself as not just an aerospace company but also an AI one before going public, with CEO Elon Musk promising investors that it would start generating $1 trillion in annual revenue before the end of the decade. Even more incredibly, the company predicted it would potentially make $26.5 trillion in AI sales down the line — more than the GDP of the entire nation of China.
“It’s already a bubble,” Gary Gensler, an MIT economist and the former head of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, told CNN this week.
Gensler pointed to the mountains of cash being poured into AI infrastructure, which some estimates put as high as $800 billion a year.
“History tells us that when you have a new technology and a significant investment… you come to a point where it plateaus. It retrenches,” said Gensler. “The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic.”
The performance of Anthropic’s newly minted stock, which investors hoped would deliver tech stocks out of a weekslong rally , is no less concerning. Insider investors immediately cashed in on the initial rally and sent its stock into free-fall, tumbling by 12 percent today. It echoed into other tech stocks, sending the Nasdaq down by 3.7 percent.
“I can’t say exactly when and how stormy,” Gensler said of the looming threat of a bursting bubble, “but I would be battening down some hatches and making sure you have some proper rain gear.”
